message.content:
**Hydrogen (H)** – the simplest and most abundant element in the universe.  
Below is a quick‑reference snapshot of its key properties, grouped into physical, chemical, and nuclear categories.

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Identity** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Isotopes | Protium (^1H), Deuterium (^2H), Tritium (^3H) |
| **Physical Properties (at STP)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ (≈0.0000899 kg m⁻³) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| | Specific heat (gas) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Diffusivity | Extremely high (≈0.61 cm² s⁻¹ at 25 °C) |
| | Solubility in water | 1.6 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ (≈0.0016 M) |
| **Chemical Properties** | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | First ionization energy | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Electron affinity | 72.8 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Bond dissociation energy (H–H) | 432 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Typical oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride) |
| | Reactivity | Highly flammable; reacts with halogens, oxygen, and many metals to form hydrides; forms acids (e.g., HCl, H₂SO₄) when combined with nonmetals |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (pKa ≈ 35) in aqueous solution; forms hydronium ions (H₃O⁺) |
| | Hydride formation | Forms ionic hydrides with alkali/alkaline earth metals (e.g., NaH, CaH₂) |
| | Hydrogen bonding | Strong dipole–dipole interactions in H₂O, NH₃, HF, etc. |
| | Allotropes | H₂ (molecular), H₂O (water), H₂S, NH₃, etc. |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Protium (^1H) | Stable, spin ½ |
| | Deuterium (^2H) | Stable, spin 1 (nuclear magnetic resonance “D” isotope) |
| | Tritium (^3H) | Radioactive, β⁻ emitter, half‑life 12.32 yr, spin ½ |
| | Nuclear spin of ^1H | ½ (used in NMR spectroscopy) |
| | Nuclear spin of ^2H | 1 (used in D‑NMR) |
| | Nuclear spin of ^3H | ½ (used in tritium labeling) |
| **Applications & Significance** | Energy carrier | Rocket propellant (liquid hydrogen + liquid oxygen), fuel cells (proton exchange membrane) |
| | Industrial use | Ammonia synthesis (Haber process), methanol production, petroleum refining |
| | Scientific use | NMR spectroscopy (proton, deuterium), tracer studies, fusion research (deuterium–tritium reactions) |
| | Cosmological importance | Most abundant element in the universe; key player in stellar nucleosynthesis and Big Bang nucleosynthesis |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the lightest element** (atomic number 1) and exists naturally as a diatomic gas (H₂) under normal conditions.
- It has **three stable isotopes**: protium (^1H), deuterium (^2H), and tritium (^3H). Tritium is radioactive and used in nuclear fusion experiments.
- Physically, it is **colorless, odorless, and extremely light**, with a very low boiling point (-252.87 °C) and melting point (-259.16 °C).
- Chemically, hydrogen is **highly reactive**: it forms covalent bonds with many elements, reacts violently with oxygen and halogens, and can act as both an acid (when protonated) and a base (as hydride, H⁻).
- Its **electronegativity (2.20)** places it in the middle of the periodic table, making it versatile in forming both ionic and covalent compounds.
- In **energy technology**, hydrogen is a clean fuel (produces only water when combusted) and is central to fuel‑cell and rocket propulsion systems.
- In **analytical chemistry**, the proton (^1H) and deuterium (^2H) nuclei are exploited in NMR spectroscopy to probe molecular structure.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
